The code calls `repartition(100)` before the write to limit the number of files, but each of the 100 tasks holds rows for many dates and writes into many date directories, so the job produces about 30,000 files of a few MB. Which fix addresses the cause?

choices.text: Replace `repartition(100)` with `coalesce(1)` so that the whole backfill is written by one task
Switch the partition column to `event_timestamp` so that every task writes into one directory only
Enable optimized writes and drop the manual repartition, so rows are shuffled by partition value and each date gets fewer, larger files
Raise the manual repartition from 100 to 1000 so each task holds fewer rows, and keep it directly before the write

stem: An append-only streaming job on a Unity Catalog managed table shows latency spikes after every commit. The job's cluster configuration enables auto compaction explicitly with the legacy Spark setting, so the writing cluster executes a short compaction step right after each successful write, and the team needs predictable micro-batch latency. They want compaction to keep working. What is the best change?

choices.text: Turn off auto compaction in the job's session and let predictive optimization compact the table asynchronously
Disable predictive optimization on the schema, because it is the feature that blocks the writing cluster after each commit
Set `delta.targetFileSize` to the smallest allowed value, so that the compaction after each commit has no files to merge
Disable all compaction features on the table and run a manual `OPTIMIZE` once each quarter, when queries become slow

stem: Analysts query a heavily normalized (third normal form) model in the lakehouse: a typical dashboard query joins nine tables and filters on attributes of a distant lookup table, and plans often scan far more data than necessary. The team can redesign the gold layer. Which direction does Databricks recommend for a new analytical model?

choices.text: Keep third normal form and add informational foreign keys, because declared constraints make the optimizer prune files by following the relationship graph
Model a star schema with a fact table at the event grain and denormalized dimension tables, so there are fewer joins and filters can skip files
Flatten everything into one wide table with every dimension attribute copied in, because storage is cheap and dimension tables are unnecessary
Split each dimension into many small tables joined by surrogate keys so each table stays tiny, since many small joins always beat a few large scans

stem: A fact table `fact_sales` declares `FOREIGN KEY (customer_sk) REFERENCES dim_customer`, and `dim_customer` declares a primary key on `customer_sk`. A late-arriving fact row with `customer_sk = 987654` is written before the customer exists. The write succeeds, and a BI report that inner-joins the two tables silently drops the sale. How should the pipeline be designed?

choices.text: Rely on the constraint but add `ENFORCED` to the foreign key, so Unity Catalog rejects the orphan row in the next run
Remove the key declarations from both tables, since the informational constraints are what lets rows be written without a dimension
Make the BI report use a left join with `COALESCE` on every column, because the foreign key then repairs missing dimension rows when the report runs
Handle orphans in the pipeline with an inferred or unknown dimension member, or quarantine, plus quality checks, as keys are not enforced

stem: `dim_customer` is an SCD Type 2 table with columns `customer_id`, `segment`, `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`, which has several rows per customer. A report joins `fact_orders` to it with `ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id` and revenue by segment is inflated for customers who changed segment. What is the correct modeling fix?

choices.text: Convert the dimension to SCD Type 1 and overwrite the segment in place, so every order shows the latest segment and history is dropped
Add `DISTINCT` to the final `SELECT` so that duplicate fact rows disappear from the revenue totals
Join on the business key and restrict to the version valid at the order date using `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`
Add a primary key constraint on `customer_id` of the dimension, so the join returns only one match per key because the engine enforces uniqueness

stem: Finance dashboards read a 4-billion-row `fact_orders` table. Three dashboards need revenue by (day, region), by (day, product) and by (day, region, product), and one of them needs average order value. The team plans materialized views and wants as few as possible with correct results for any roll-up. Which design fits?

choices.text: One materialized view at (day, region, product) storing `SUM(revenue)` and `COUNT(*)`, with dashboards computing the average as a ratio of sums
A materialized view that stores `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` per group, and dashboards add those counts to get customers per coarser grain
Three standard views with the same queries, since a standard view keeps its result stored in a table and so is faster than a materialized view
One view per dashboard storing `AVG(order_value)` for each grain, because averages can be summed later when a user selects a coarser grain

stem: Three teams report "revenue per active customer", each in its own standard view that groups by region and divides revenue by distinct customers. A fourth team groups the same view by product and gets numbers that cannot be compared with the others, and the average of regional ratios does not equal the global ratio. The company wants one governed definition that every team can group by any dimension. What should the data engineer build?

choices.text: A Unity Catalog metric view that defines the ratio measure once, with dimensions as fields, queried with `MEASURE()`
A shared notebook with the formula that each team copies into its own views, adjusted to its grouping when needed
A table with one row per region that a nightly job writes with the ratio, so every team reads the same number
One materialized view per team that stores the regional ratio as a column, plus a policy that teams average the stored ratios

stem: A metric view uses `fact_orders` as its source and joins `dim_customer`, an SCD Type 2 table with several rows per `customer_id`, on `customer_id`. Revenue by customer segment is wrong for customers who changed segment: the numbers show only one version of the segment. What explains the result and what is the fix?

choices.text: Metric view measures are always evaluated on the dimension table, so revenue is attributed to the segment of the dimension row stored last
The join is many-to-many and the engine takes the first matching row; join a source query with one row per customer
Metric views reject joins to Type 2 tables, so the engine copies the fact table first; replace the join with an `INNER JOIN` in the dashboard
The metric view repeated the fact rows for each version of the dimension, so a measure should divide revenue by the number of versions

stem: A team has a gold materialized view that cleans, joins and denormalizes orders for performance and wants to publish governed KPIs to dashboards, notebooks and AI assistants. A colleague proposes to put the KPI logic inside the same materialized view as extra aggregated columns. What is the better division of responsibilities?

choices.text: Move the heavy joins into a standard view and define the KPIs in the materialized view, because a standard view is always faster than stored results
Drop the materialized view and put all cleaning, joining and denormalizing logic into the metric view, since metric views replace transformation tables
Keep both in the materialized view, because a materialized view can store several groupings at once and so also serves as the semantic layer
Keep the materialized view as the stored layer and define a metric view on top, so measures and fields are defined once

stem: A gold table `fact_orders` stores one row per order line. It also carries the order-level `shipping_fee`, repeated on every line of the order. Finance reports `SUM(shipping_fee)` that is far higher than the invoiced shipping, while `SUM(line_amount)` is correct. What design change fixes the model?

choices.text: Divide `shipping_fee` by the largest `line_number` in every report, because the repeated lines are a reporting issue only
Add a primary key on `order_id` in the fact table, so the engine removes the repeated shipping values at query time
Keep each fact table at one declared grain: move the shipping fee to an order-level fact table or allocate it to lines in the load
Keep the table, but change `shipping_fee` to a `DOUBLE` type, so repeated values are no longer added together

stem: A data steward holds `MANAGE` on the catalog `lab` and has no other privileges, no ownership and no admin role. The steward runs `GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG lab TO steward`, which succeeds, but `SELECT * FROM lab.exp.runs` still fails with a permission error. What is missing, and what is the fix?

choices.text: `MANAGE` blocks the steward from holding data privileges at the same time, so the steward must first give up `MANAGE` and ask an owner to grant `SELECT`
`SELECT` on a catalog inherits only to schemas and never to tables, so the steward must repeat the grant on every table of the schema `lab.exp`
A self-grant takes effect only after another account admin approves it, so the steward must wait until an admin confirms the new privilege
Data privileges also need the usage privileges on the parents, so the steward grants themselves `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA`, which `MANAGE` allows

stem: A group of data stewards must read volume files and query tables in every schema of the catalog `corp`, including schemas created later. An admin grants the group `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` on the catalog `corp`. Tables work, but listing files in the volume `corp.raw.landing` fails with a permission error. Which change fixes this with the least maintenance?

choices.text: Grant `READ FILES` on the metastore, since metastore-level privileges inherit to all volumes in every catalog and need no extra usage privileges
Grant `SELECT` on the volume `corp.raw.landing`, because the volume is a child of the schema and `SELECT` is the privilege that covers every data object type
Grant `READ VOLUME` on the catalog `corp` to the group, because `SELECT` does not apply to volumes and `READ VOLUME` inherits to current and future volumes
Make the group owner of the volume `corp.raw.landing`, because ownership of a child object is inherited by the parent catalog and then covers all other volumes

stem: A nightly job on a classic cluster takes three times longer than expected. In the Spark UI the jobs timeline shows many gaps of several minutes with no Spark job running. The cluster Metrics view shows one machine, the driver, in red and all workers in blue. The code launches 40 concurrent Structured Streaming queries from threads and loops in plain Python between them. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Reduce the concurrent queries, move them to separate compute or choose a larger driver node type, and rewrite the Python loops with Spark
Enable autoscaling on the workers, because the red driver tile is Spark reporting that the executors need to scale out
Add more workers to the cluster, because idle workers in the timeline mean the cluster has too little parallelism for the stages
Increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` so each stage creates more tasks, because the gaps are the time between oversized shuffle stages

stem: A batch job on an autoscaling classic cluster finishes successfully but slower than usual. The Spark UI shows executors being removed several times during the run, and a colleague suspects out-of-memory crashes. What is the right first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Query `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline`, which stores one row per executor removal with the termination code of the executor and the node that hosted it
Read the compute Event log for resize or lost-instance events: autoscaling removals are expected, spot reclaims show up there, and only unexplained ones point to memory
Increase the driver node type first, because executors are removed whenever the driver heap fills with task metadata, and then rerun the job to compare
Open the Streaming tab of the Spark UI, which lists each removed executor with its exception and the batch it served

stem: Job clusters are terminated after each run. After a failure at night the on-call engineer needs the driver and worker logs, but the cluster is gone and the compute's Event log tab holds only lifecycle events. The platform team asks how to make Spark logs available for later analysis. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Download the compute Event log as CSV after each failure, because it includes the driver stack trace and the executor stderr output
Configure a log delivery location for the compute, so driver and worker logs are delivered to storage that outlives the cluster
Query `system.compute.node_timeline`, which stores the log4j and stdout text of each node at minute granularity for later searches
Give the engineers access to the Executors tab of the Spark UI, because it keeps the worker log files of terminated clusters indefinitely

stem: A platform engineer wants to list jobs whose runs were repaired, with the number of repairs per run, using `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline`. Runs longer than one hour are stored as several hourly rows. Which query logic counts repairs correctly?

choices.text: Count rows with a non-null `result_state` per `run_id` and subtract one, as only the last row of each attempt has a result
Count rows where `termination_code` is not `SUCCESS`, because every repair attempt is preceded by a failed row for that run
Count all rows per `run_id` and subtract one, because every repair adds one hourly slice row to the table
Group by `job_id` and count distinct `run_id` values, because a repair creates a new run identifier for the same job

stem: Analysts report that scheduled runs of a job were "skipped overnight". In `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline` the affected runs appear with `period_start_time` equal to `period_end_time`, and no compute is listed. Which column should the engineer inspect to find out why the runs did not start?

choices.text: `trigger_type`, because the trigger of a skipped run records the reason the scheduler declined to start it
`result_state`, because a run that never started has a state that names the missing cluster or the quota that was exceeded
`compute_ids`, because an empty array proves that the cluster failed to start and lists the failed node types
`termination_code`, because a row with equal start and end time shows a run that never began and the code explains why

stem: A job task runs a SQL statement on a shared SQL warehouse and its duration has doubled. In `system.query.history`, filtered through `query_source` to that task run, the statement shows `execution_duration_ms` about the same as before but `waiting_at_capacity_duration_ms` of several minutes. What is the conclusion and the remedy?

choices.text: The statement is waiting for the warehouse cluster to start up, so keep the warehouse running permanently and the wait will go away completely
The statement is executing slowly because of data skew, so rewrite the join with a salted key and rebuild the table with Liquid Clustering
The statement is queued for compute capacity, so add warehouse capacity (size or clusters) or reduce competing load rather than tune the SQL
The statement is blocked by lock contention in the Delta transaction log, so serialize all writers of the table in one single job at night

stem: A nightly job on a jobs cluster fails with a driver out-of-memory error at different points of the run. The engineer wants evidence from system tables about how the nodes were loaded in the minutes before the failure, with per-node resolution. Which table and reading support the diagnosis?

choices.text: `system.lakeflow.job_task_run_timeline`: per-minute memory use per task, so tasks with the longest period show the memory pressure on the driver or workers
`system.compute.node_types`: a time series of memory pressure per node type, from which a driver bottleneck follows if the instance family is memory optimized
`system.query.history`: peak driver heap use for every statement, which shows how close the driver came to its limit before it was lost
`system.compute.node_timeline`: per-minute CPU and memory per instance with a `driver` flag, so a driver near its memory limit and low workers show a driver bottleneck

stem: A stage of a nightly batch job on a classic cluster runs 14 minutes, while 199 of its 200 tasks finish in about 20 seconds. The stage page shows no spill. Summary Metrics show a Max duration far above the 75th percentile. The stage belongs to a sort merge join, adaptive query execution is on, and the largest shuffle partition is smaller than the default skew thresholds. Which action addresses the cause?

choices.text: Add more workers to the cluster, because 199 cores sit idle and the extra cores will take over part of the long running task
Lower the AQE skew settings `skewedPartitionFactor` and `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` so that the oversized partition is detected and split
Force a broadcast hint on the larger side of the join, because broadcast joins are always optimized for skewed keys by AQE
Increase the executor memory of the cluster, because the long task is slow when executors run out of execution memory during the join

stem: A notebook starts a Structured Streaming query on an all-purpose cluster, and a few minutes later the developer opens the Spark UI and finds no Streaming tab. The cell showed no error. Which conclusion and next step fit?

choices.text: The tab appears only when a streaming job runs on the compute, so the stream probably never started; read the driver logs for the exception
Streaming metrics are shown only in the SQL tab for Structured Streaming, so the missing tab is expected and means nothing
The tab is hidden for Standard access mode, so the developer must switch the compute to Dedicated mode to see processing times
The tab appears only after a minimum of 100 completed batches, so the developer should keep waiting and refresh the page

stem: A job has the tasks `ingest` → `transform` → `publish`. The run failed in `transform` because its notebook path pointed to a moved file, and `publish` shows "Upstream failed". `ingest` succeeded and uses a job cluster shared by all three tasks. The engineer edits the `transform` task to the new path and starts a repair run. What happens?

choices.text: `transform` and `publish` run again with the path stored in the original run, because a repair restores the settings of that run
All three tasks run again, because a repair after a settings change must start from the root task to stay consistent
`transform` and `publish` run with the updated settings on a new copy of the shared job cluster, and `ingest` is not run again
Only `transform` runs again with the new path, and `publish` stays in its failed state until the next scheduled run

stem: An operator started a run with Run now and typed `run_date = 2026-10-31` instead of `2026-11-01`. `ingest` and `transform` succeeded and wrote data for 31 October, then `publish` failed on an unrelated permission problem that is now fixed. The operator plans to repair the run and enter the corrected `run_date` in the repair dialog. What is wrong with this plan?

choices.text: The value reaches only re-run tasks, so `ingest` and `transform` keep their 31 October output; a new run with the correct parameter is needed
The repair dialog replaces the value for the whole run, so `ingest` and `transform` would re-run automatically and write the new date twice
The value entered during a repair is stored only if the job owner approves it, so the corrected value would be ignored by the repaired task
Parameters can be edited in a repair only before the first repair of a run, and a failed `publish` has already been attempted once

stem: During an incident the team disabled the task `quality_gate` in the job `load_dim`. The dependent task `load` (Run if: at least one succeeded) still ran in that run and failed. The cause is fixed and `quality_gate` is enabled again. The engineer wants the repair to execute `quality_gate` as well. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Re-enabling the task is enough, because a repair always re-evaluates the disabled flag and runs every task that was skipped in the original run
The task runs automatically because disabled tasks count as failed, so `rerun_all_failed_tasks` already includes it
A disabled task can run only in a new run, because the Jobs API rejects `rerun_tasks` entries for tasks that were disabled in the original run
A repair works from run state, not the disabled setting, so `quality_gate` must be named in `rerun_tasks`

stem: A job `rebuild_marts` has the job parameter `target_schema` with the default `staging`. Compliance wants evidence that nobody can run the job against `prod_marts`. Analysts hold CAN MANAGE RUN on the job so they can start it. A lead states that the default value protects the production schema. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Overrides of job parameters are rejected by the Jobs API unless the parameter is marked as editable in the job definition, and the default is not marked
CAN MANAGE RUN allows a run with other parameters, so the default is no control; restrict permissions or validate in code
Only the job owner can supply different parameter values with Run now, so analysts can start the job but cannot change the schema
Job parameter values can be changed only through a repair, which needs CAN MANAGE, so analysts holding CAN MANAGE RUN cannot use it at all

stem: A continuous job processes a queue. After a source outage it failed repeatedly, and the job now shows an exponential backoff state with a long wait before the next retry. The source has recovered and the team wants processing to resume immediately. What should they do?

choices.text: Increase the maximum concurrent runs of the job to 2, so that a second run starts without waiting for the backoff period
Use Repair run on the last failed run, because a repair resets the retry period of a continuous job as it starts the failed tasks
Use Restart run, which restarts the continuous job at once instead of waiting for the backoff period to end
Click Run now to start another run beside the waiting one, because the retry delay applies only to runs started by the scheduler

stem: A bundle-deployed job `nightly_load` has the job parameter `run_date` and the tasks `ingest` → `transform` → `publish`. Operations must backfill `2026-11-01` by running `transform` and everything that depends on it, without running `ingest` again, from a CI step. Which command fits?

choices.text: `databricks bundle run --only transform+ --params run_date=2026-11-01 nightly_load`, which starts a new run of the task and its dependents
`databricks bundle deploy --params run_date=2026-11-01`, which stores the new date and then repairs the last failed run of the job
`databricks bundle run nightly_load --notebook-params run_date=2026-11-01`, which passes the date to all notebook tasks of the job as widgets
`databricks bundle run --only transform --params run_date=2026-11-01 nightly_load`, which runs the task and its downstream tasks

stem: A Lakeflow pipeline with six streaming tables reads a Kafka topic that keeps seven days of data, while the tables hold two years of history. One update failed in a single streaming table because of a transient storage error, and the cause is fixed. Which remediation avoids losing data?

choices.text: Delete the failed table and let the next update recreate it, because the new table automatically backfills history from the Kafka topic
Start a full refresh of the whole pipeline, since it recomputes every table from the sources and so repairs the failed one
Use a full refresh selection of the failed table, because it clears only that table's checkpoint and keeps the existing rows
Start an update of only the failed tables (Refresh failed tables) with default refresh semantics, which also updates the dependents

stem: A bundle's `staging` target sets `presets: {trigger_pause_status: PAUSED}` so schedules from the bundle stay paused. The job `nightly_dq` in the bundle declares `schedule: {quartz_cron_expression: ..., pause_status: UNPAUSED}`. After `databricks bundle deploy -t staging`, what is the state of the `nightly_dq` schedule?

choices.text: Paused, until the deployer adds `--force`, which lets resource settings replace presets on the command line
Paused, because a target preset is applied last and overrides settings that are written in a resource
Unpaused, because settings in an individual resource override presets, so only the other schedules stay paused
The deployment fails with a conflict error, because a preset and a resource may not both set `pause_status`

stem: A CI runner was killed during `databricks bundle deploy -t prod`. Every later deployment of the bundle now fails because it cannot acquire the deployment lock. The team has confirmed that no deployment is actually running. What is the correct action?

choices.text: Set `bundle.deployment.lock.enabled: false` in the prod target permanently, so no deployment ever waits for a lock again
Redeploy once with `--force-lock`, which forces lock acquisition and is meant for a stale lock left by an interrupted deployment
Redeploy with `--force`, which overrides all blocking validations, including the lock left by the interrupted deployment
Delete the bundle's folder in the workspace so the next deployment starts clean and without any old lock file, then deploy again

stem: A release pipeline deploys a bundle to `prod`. Jobs that run on a schedule might still be executing when the pipeline starts, and the team does not want the deployment to update jobs and pipelines while runs are in flight. Which option expresses this?

choices.text: `databricks bundle plan -t prod`, which blocks the following deployment while any resource in the plan has a run in progress
`databricks bundle deploy -t prod --auto-approve`, which waits for active runs because it answers approval prompts with a delay
`databricks bundle deploy -t prod --force`, which cancels active runs before the resources are updated
`databricks bundle deploy -t prod --fail-on-active-runs`, which fails the deployment when jobs or pipelines in it have active runs

stem: A bundle sets the group `data-eng` to `CAN_VIEW` in the top-level `permissions` mapping. A developer also adds `data-eng` with `CAN_MANAGE_RUN` under the permissions of the job `nightly_load` so operators can start it. The configuration is no longer accepted. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Top-level permissions apply to all resources, so a resource may add only weaker levels, and the job entry should use `CAN_VIEW`
One principal cannot get permissions both at the top level and inside a resource, so define the group in one place only, for example at the job
Permission levels such as `CAN_MANAGE_RUN` are valid only for users, so the group entry must be replaced by individual user names
Resource-level permissions are valid only in the `targets` mapping, so the job entry must be moved under the target, with a different level

stem: The `prod` target of a bundle sets `run_as` to a service principal. The bundle contains a job, a pipeline and an AI/BI dashboard. A release engineer deploys with their own user identity and the validation reports that some resources are not supported with this combination. What is the most robust change?

choices.text: Deploy from CI as the service principal named in `run_as`, so deploying and run identity are the same and every resource type is supported
Add `--force` to the deploy command, which lets the dashboard take over the identity of the deployer instead of the service principal
Give the engineer `CAN_USE` on the service principal, which extends `run_as` support to all resource types in the bundle, dashboards included
Set `mode: development` on the target, because only development mode supports `run_as` for dashboards and other resource types

stem: A bundle deploys an AI/BI dashboard from `dash/sales.lvdash.json`. An analyst edits the deployed dashboard in the workspace UI. The next CI deployment of the bundle fails with an error about the dashboard. The edits should be kept. What should the team do?

choices.text: Run `databricks bundle deployment unbind` for the dashboard resource, which keeps the remote edits and makes the next deployment succeed
Remove the dashboard from the bundle, deploy, and add it back, which preserves the edits made in the UI
Run `databricks bundle generate dashboard --resource <key>` to download the workspace version into the bundle, commit it, then deploy
Run `databricks bundle deploy --force` so that the dashboard in the workspace is merged with the local file

stem: A team renames `bundle.name` from `sales_etl` to `sales_platform` and deploys to `prod`. Afterwards the workspace holds two sets of jobs, both with active schedules, and the old copies still run. Which statement explains the cause and gives the cleanest way to avoid it?

choices.text: Renaming the bundle deletes the lock file of the old deployment, which starts the new one in parallel; deploy again after waiting for the lock timeout to expire
A bundle matches resources by display name, so renaming the jobs in YAML in the same commit would have kept the old ones; edit the job names back
Identity is name, target and workspace, with state in the deployment folder, so a rename is a new deployment; bind the new keys to the old job IDs or destroy the old one
The deployer must run `databricks bundle validate --migrate` to carry state over to the new name, which was skipped in this case

stem: Five developers edit notebooks in one shared Git folder checked out on the branch `main`. Their uncommitted edits collide, commits go straight to `main` and nobody reviews them. The team wants a flow that follows the recommended Git folders practice. What should they do?

choices.text: Each developer clones the repository into a Git folder under their own user folder, works on a personal branch, pushes it and opens a pull request into the deployment branch
Create one feature branch inside the shared folder for the whole team, so that all five developers commit to that branch and a single review covers the work
Keep the shared folder but give everyone Can Edit and ask developers to pull `main` before each edit, so that collisions are resolved before they start typing
Let each developer edit the notebooks directly in the production Git folder, because a pull request is created automatically from the changed files of that folder

stem: A job has three tasks that all point at notebooks in a workspace Git folder. A sync job pulls the folder at 02:00, and the data job runs at 01:55 for about 15 minutes, so the sync lands while the run is active. Some tasks of one run execute old code and others new code. Which change addresses the cause?

choices.text: Give each task its own Git folder with a separate branch, so tasks cannot see each other's code changes during one run
Configure the job to use the remote Git repository with a branch, tag or commit, so the run snapshots it and all tasks use one commit
Move the sync job to 01:50 so the pull always completes before the data job starts, and keep the notebooks in the Git folder
Keep the Git folder and set the maximum concurrent runs of the data job to 1, so that no run of it can overlap with the sync job

stem: A job task is switched from a notebook in a workspace Git folder to the remote Git repository source with a branch. The next run fails in a notebook that writes an intermediate CSV file to a relative path in the workspace files area of the task. The notebook worked before the switch. What explains this, and what is the fix?

choices.text: The remote Git source runs notebooks only in read-only sessions of the whole job, so the job must go back to the workspace Git folder for any task that writes data
The task lacks a Git credential for pushing the new file, so the engineer must create a personal access token that lets the task commit the CSV to the branch
The relative path resolves against the commit snapshot, which Databricks locks for 24 hours, so the task must wait until the lock on the commit expires
Tasks that use a remote Git repository cannot write to workspace files, so write temporary data to driver ephemeral storage and persistent data to a volume or table

stem: A column mask ABAC policy on the catalog `fin` matches every column tagged `sensitivity` and calls `mask_all(v STRING) RETURNS STRING`, which returns `'REDACTED'`. Stewards then tag a `DOUBLE` column `salary` and a `DATE` column `birth_date`. Queries on those tables now fail for users the policy applies to, while masked `STRING` columns work. The team wants to keep a single policy. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Replace it with a `VARIANT` based function that branches on `schema_of_variant()` and returns a value castable to the column type, such as `0.0` or a fixed date
Add the affected users to the policy's `EXCEPT` clause for tables that contain numeric or date columns, so the mask function is not evaluated for them at all
Re-create the function as a Python UDF in Unity Catalog, because the engine does not cast the return value of Python UDFs and so accepts `'REDACTED'` for any type
Mark `mask_all` as `DETERMINISTIC`, because a function that is not declared deterministic cannot be cast to the type of the column it masks

stem: An analytics team pseudonymizes the 10-digit `phone_number` column with `sha2(phone_number, 256)` and states in its documentation that the data is anonymized. A reviewer shows that the original numbers can be recovered by hashing every possible number and comparing. Tables from several systems must still be joinable on the pseudonym. Which change addresses the weakness?

choices.text: Keep the plain hash and add a column mask that shows the hash only to members of the analytics group, hiding it from everyone else
Hash the number with a secret key kept outside the data plus a version number, so output stays deterministic for joins but cannot be recomputed from guesses
Switch the digest to `sha2(phone_number, 512)`, because a longer digest cannot be reversed by hashing the candidate numbers
Replace the hash with `uuid()` generated per row, since a random value cannot be recomputed from the phone number by anyone who holds the original

stem: Analysts study the age distribution and regional sales of customers. The `customers` table has the exact `birth_date` and a full postal code. Privacy counsel wants a lower re-identification risk, and nobody in the analytics group needs exact values. Which method fits the need?

choices.text: Replace `birth_date` and the postal code with salted hashes, because a hashed value hides the original and the analysts can still group by it
Tokenize both columns with random tokens held in a restricted mapping table, so that analysts can look up the original values when needed
Generalize the values: expose an age band computed from `birth_date` and only the first digits of the postal code, so each group has many people
Suppress both columns by returning `NULL` in a mask for the analytics group, since the group does not need individual attributes

stem: A product events table with billions of rows carries `email`. Support agents must occasionally re-identify a customer, analytics must join events across systems, and a right-to-erasure request must make a customer's events non-attributable without rewriting the large events table. Which design meets all three?

choices.text: Replace the email with a generalized domain value such as the part after `@`, which groups customers and needs no mapping table for erasure
Keep the plain email and attach a column mask that returns `'***'` for analysts, then run `DELETE` on the events table for each erasure request
Replace the email with `sha2(email, 256)` at ingestion, and on an erasure request delete the customer from the source system so the hash can no longer be matched
Replace the email with a random token at ingestion, keep the token-to-email mapping in a tightly restricted table, and on an erasure request delete the mapping row

stem: A team runs `CREATE TABLE dev.crm.customers DEEP CLONE prod.crm.customers` to give developers realistic data. The prod table has column masks from ABAC policies on its PII columns, and the statement fails for regular users. The developers must not see raw PII in dev. Which approach achieves this?

choices.text: Add the developers to the `EXCEPT` clause of the policy so they can clone the table, then mask the columns again in the dev catalog
Run the deep clone as the owner of the prod table and attach the same ABAC policies in dev, so developers see masked values in the clone
Point a dev external table at the Delta files of the prod table, so developers read the same files through their own governed dev catalog
Build the dev table with a job that reads prod as an exempt principal and writes anonymized values (hashed, generalized or suppressed) into dev

stem: Partners drop JSON events in cloud storage. Bronze is loaded with Auto Loader using `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = rescue`; silver selects named columns and masks `email` and `phone`. One partner starts sending a new field `national_id`. Compliance asks where the field lands and whether silver is still compliant. What is the correct assessment?

choices.text: The stream keeps running and `national_id` sits unmasked in bronze inside `_rescued_data`, so that column needs the same protection as other identifiers
Auto Loader adds `national_id` to the schema automatically and a masking policy already covers it because policies apply to new columns
The new field is dropped silently because it is not in the schema, so no unmasked identifier is stored anywhere in the lakehouse
The stream fails with `UnknownFieldException` until restarted, after which `national_id` becomes a bronze column that silver then ignores

stem: A pipeline masks `ssn` before writing the silver table. Compliance requires that no record with an unmasked value (a nine-digit pattern) ever reaches silver, that other records continue to flow, and that offending records are kept for investigation by a small group. Which approach meets all three?

choices.text: Use `expect_or_drop` on the pattern check, because dropped rows are logged and the offending records can be read back from the event log
Add a pattern expectation on the masked column, route offending rows to a restricted quarantine table, and feed silver only from rows that pass
Use the default `expect` on the pattern check, which flags violating rows in the metrics and keeps them out of the target table
Use `expect_or_fail` on the pattern check, so the update stops and rolls back when a violating row appears, protecting silver completely

stem: A catalog-level ABAC policy masks `email` for `account users`. A Lakeflow job runs as the service principal `sp_etl`, which is not exempt, and writes `silver.customers` with `email_token = sha2(email, 256)` read from bronze. After the policy was added every `email_token` in silver is identical, and joins on it collapse. How should the pipeline be fixed?

choices.text: Run the job as a user in the compliance group, because their identity is already exempt from the masking policy on bronze
Hash the email inside the policy's masking function and have the job read the hashed value instead of the original
Add `sp_etl` to the policy's `EXCEPT` clause, keep bronze restricted, compute the token in the job, and tag silver for its own policy
Remove the policy from bronze so the job sees real emails, and rely on the hashed token in silver to protect the email values everywhere in the lakehouse

stem: Data Classification is enabled on a catalog and detects email addresses and phone numbers in new tables. A steward wants to review the sample values behind detections, but the platform admin proposes granting `SELECT` on `system.data_classification.results` to the whole data-engineering department so everyone can browse detections. What is the appropriate decision?

choices.text: Grant it, because classification results contain only column names and counts, which carry no sensitive information
Copy it into each catalog, because then engineers read only the samples for the catalog they work in
Share it only with the stewards who may see metastore-wide results, because it includes sample values from tables in every catalog
Grant it, because the table is filtered by privilege so each engineer sees only detections in catalogs they can already read

stem: A streaming job deduplicates events with `withWatermark("event_time", "1 day").dropDuplicates(["email", "event_id"])` and writes to a Delta table that has masking. A privacy review finds raw emails in the checkpoint directory in cloud storage, outside the reach of table masks and of the erasure `DELETE`. How should the job be changed?

choices.text: Add a column mask on the sink table, because masks also apply to the state that the stream stores in its checkpoint
Replace `email` by a keyed token in a projection before `dropDuplicates`, so the state holds only tokens
Reduce the watermark to one hour, which makes the raw emails leave the stream state after a shorter time
Run `VACUUM` on the sink table after each erasure, since vacuum also removes files under the checkpoint folder

stem: A managed table has deletion vectors enabled. For an erasure request the team ran `DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 42` and, in the same hour, `VACUUM customers`. A later audit still finds the customer's row in the Parquet files in storage. What explains this, and what completes the erasure?

choices.text: The delete wrote only a deletion vector, so the file still holds the row; run `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)`, then `VACUUM` once old files pass retention
Deletion vectors must be disabled with `ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES`, which rewrites all files at once and removes the row from storage
Run `VACUUM customers LITE`, which reads the transaction log and deletes data files that still contain rows marked as deleted
The `VACUUM` ran too early in the day; running it again after 24 hours removes every file that contained the deleted row, whatever the retention

stem: A bronze table has Change Data Feed enabled and keeps the default history. After `DELETE FROM bronze.orders WHERE customer_id = 7`, a privacy officer asks where the customer's values can still be found in storage and when they leave. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Only older table versions are affected, because the change feed keeps row keys but not values, so the feed needs no separate cleanup step
Nothing remains, because Delta blocks time travel and change feed reads for any version that contains a deleted row once the delete commits
Only the `_change_data` files hold them, and these are never removed by `VACUUM`, so the feed must be deleted by hand after each erasure
Older versions kept for time travel hold them, and `_change_data` files record the delete with row values; `VACUUM` removes both past retention

stem: Legal requires that erased personal data leaves cloud storage within 14 days. A weekly backfill job writes to the table for up to three days. An engineer proposes `SET spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false` followed by `VACUUM events RETAIN 0 HOURS` after every erasure. Which design meets the deadline with the least risk?

choices.text: Raise `deletedFileRetentionDuration` to 30 days to protect rollbacks and rely on the log retention to meet the deadline
The proposal itself, because it removes files immediately and time travel is not needed for erasure
Keep the retention at 7 days, above the longest writer, and run delete, any needed purge and a scheduled `VACUUM`, so files are gone after about a week
Set `logRetentionDuration` to 1 day, since removing transaction log entries makes the old data files unreachable and so deletes them from storage

stem: The streaming table `silver_events` reads a Kafka topic with seven days of retention and holds two years of history. An erasure request names one subject. An engineer plans to delete the subject at the source and then fully refresh `silver_events` to rebuild it without the subject. What should the team do instead?

choices.text: Run a full refresh of the streaming table, because it clears the state and reprocesses everything from the topic including the older history
Delete the subject's rows from the streaming table with DML, keep the stream running, and also remove the subject upstream where the platform allows it
Drop and re-create the table from the topic, since a new table is built only from the data that still exists upstream
Add `skipChangeCommits` to the Kafka read, so the stream skips the deleted rows and continues without failing

stem: About 400 erasure requests arrive daily. The current job runs `DELETE FROM events WHERE user_id = <id>` once per request against a very large `events` table. Each statement rewrites many files, the job runs for hours, and concurrent runs conflict. Which redesign is the most efficient?

choices.text: Run the 400 `DELETE` statements in parallel threads from one notebook, so that every request finishes together within a few minutes
Run `VACUUM` after each request with a retention of zero hours, so that the old files holding the rows never accumulate
Add an `is_deleted` flag set by a single `UPDATE` for all requested users and filter flagged rows out in a view for readers
Collect requests in a control table, run one `MERGE ... WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE` per cycle on a table clustered by `user_id`, then mark done

stem: A data steward holds `SELECT`, `MODIFY`, `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` on the catalog `prod` through grants, and owns none of its objects. Setting a description with `COMMENT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders IS '...'` works, but `COMMENT ON VIEW prod.sales.v_orders IS '...'` fails with a permission error. What is the reason?

choices.text: Editing the comment of a view requires being the owner of the view; table privileges and even `MANAGE` do not replace ownership
Comments on views need `MANAGE` on the view's schema in addition to the table privileges, and the steward holds no `MANAGE` anywhere
Views cannot carry comments in Unity Catalog, so descriptions must be placed in tags instead
Only the catalog owner can comment on views, because views are created at the catalog level

stem: Analysts report they cannot find the tables of the catalog `corp` in search. The data office wants every employee to see names, comments and tags of all tables in that catalog only and request access, without granting data access and without having to maintain `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` for everyone. Which grant achieves this?

choices.text: `BROWSE` on each schema of `corp` to `account users`, repeated whenever a schema is created, so every table is discoverable
`READ METADATA` on the metastore to `account users`, which exposes names, comments and tags of everything without usage privileges
`SELECT` on the catalog `corp` to `account users`, since users need read access before an object appears in search
`BROWSE` on the catalog `corp` to `account users`, which makes all its objects discoverable and keeps their data unreadable

stem: A governance lead, who holds every privilege needed to edit comments, wants Databricks AI-generated comments for the tables, their columns and the schemas of the catalog `corp`. AI-assistive features are enabled in the workspace. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Suggestions exist for every securable, but a metastore admin must approve each one in Governance Hub before it becomes visible to users
Suggestions exist for tables and table columns; schema descriptions must be written manually, for example with `COMMENT ON SCHEMA`
Suggestions exist only for schemas and catalogs, so table descriptions have to be maintained as tags instead
Suggestions are applied automatically to tables, columns and schemas, so no reviewer has to accept or edit them

stem: To track a deletion request, a steward sets the table tag `dsr_ticket = jane.doe@example.com` so that the privacy team can search for affected tables. The security reviewer asks to remove it. What is the reasoning?

choices.text: Tags are encrypted with the key of the table, so the e-mail address would be unreadable to every user who has not been granted SELECT on the table
Only governed tags are stored as plain text; an ordinary tag like this one is protected as table data, so the reviewer is mistaken
Tag values are plain text and may be replicated globally, so keep personal data out of tags; use an opaque ticket id and keep details in a restricted table
Tags are visible only to users with SELECT on the table, so the value is acceptable provided that the table is restricted

stem: The catalog `prod` is tagged `retention = 7y`. The table `prod.hr.payroll` is tagged `retention = 10y`, and its column `ssn` has no tag of its own. Which statement about how these tags behave is correct?

choices.text: A search returns the catalog and objects inheriting its tag, `payroll` uses its more specific `10y`, and the `ssn` column does not inherit the table's tags
Tags are inherited only between objects of one type, so schemas inherit from catalogs and columns from tables, but tables do not inherit from schemas
Tags apply only to the object they were set on, so a search for the catalog's tag lists the catalog alone and ignores the tables in it
Both values apply to `payroll` at the same time, and the column `ssn` inherits both from the table, so each value can match a policy condition

stem: A compliance analyst runs `SELECT * FROM system.information_schema.column_tags WHERE tag_name = 'pii'` to inventory tagged columns. It returns about 340 columns, while stewards know there are about 900 across the metastore. No query error occurs. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?

choices.text: Governed tags are excluded from the information schema and can only be exported from the account console, so the 560 missing rows are governed tags
Tag rows older than the retention of the transaction log are removed from the table, so the analyst needs to widen the log retention setting
The information schema filters results by the caller's privileges, so run the inventory as a principal that can access all catalogs
Column tags exist only in each catalog's own information schema, so the system view is incomplete and must be replaced by a UNION over every catalog

stem: A column `phone` carries a governed tag `pii`. A developer runs `ALTER TABLE crm.customers DROP COLUMN phone` and the statement fails. After the tag is removed the column is dropped, but the privacy officer wants assurance that the phone numbers are really gone. What is the correct handling?

choices.text: Keep the governed tag on the column to document the former PII, and set a retention policy on the tag so that it expires together with the data
